original.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent on a Loss Bowl: Learning Rate and Batch Size
original.description: A colored, stretched bowl-shaped surface shows the loss (the error to minimize) over two model weights, with a marked lowest point. A ball starts on the slope. Each step, it moves against a slope estimated from a small random batch of data and leaves a trail. A run lasts up to 40 steps. Change the learning rate to see steps shrink, grow, zigzag or fly out of the bowl. Change the batch size to see the path go from jittery to smooth.
original.reason: You asked to change the learning rate and batch size. Here you can set both, run a short descent step by step, and compare a saved path and the loss readouts with the current run.
interactions: Play, pause or advance one step at a time. The ball descends and leaves a trail of up to 40 points, one for each step. The run ends after 40 steps or when the ball leaves the bowl.
Learning rate: small values give short, slow steps. Above 0.25 the ball zigzags across the steep direction. Above 0.5 the zigzag grows each step and the ball can leave the bowl ("diverged").
Batch size: at 1 the steps scatter in many directions and the ball keeps jittering near the bottom. Larger batches straighten the path. At 256 every step follows the exact slope.
Full-batch direction: when this is on, a faint arrow shows the direction the full dataset would give. A solid arrow shows the batch step the ball actually takes.
Keep path and restart: the current trail (up to 40 points) becomes a faded comparison line, replacing any earlier one. The ball restarts from the same point with current settings.
assumptions: This is an illustration: the loss bowl is a made-up formula and the batch noise is simulated, not taken from a real dataset or model.

The loss is half of (first weight squared + 4 × second weight squared). Without noise, each step multiplies the distance along the steep direction by (1 − 4 × learning rate): the ball zigzags when this is negative (above 0.25) and swings wider when below −1 (above 0.5).

The batch slope is the exact slope plus simulated random noise. The noise shrinks as the batch grows, as it would when sampling without replacement from 256 examples, and is exactly zero at batch size 256.
The noise comes from a fixed seed, so after Reset the same settings give the same path.
The solid arrow is the step actually taken: the negative batch slope times the learning rate. The faint arrow is the negative full-batch slope. The ball moves along the solid arrow.

Readouts show the step count (0 to 40), the current loss, the distance from the lowest point and the batch noise level. A diverged state is shown when the ball passes the bowl's edge, and that run stops.
limitations: With small batches, a single step can raise the loss. The loss goes down only on average.
With noise, the stability values above describe the typical trend rather than every single run.
Just above 0.5 the zigzag grows slowly and may not leave the bowl within 40 steps.
Each run is limited to 40 steps, so very slow settings, such as a tiny learning rate, may not reach the bottom.
A real neural network's loss has many dimensions, flat areas and several valleys. This bowl has two weights and one lowest point.
The scene does not measure computing time, so it cannot show the extra cost of large batches.
original.learningGoal: See that SGD steps downhill using a noisy estimate of the slope from a batch of data. The learning rate sets the step length and whether the process stays stable. A larger batch reduces the noise but uses more data per step.

original.title: Stochastic gradient descent: fitting a line one mini-batch at a time
original.description: A 3D loss bowl shows how wrong a straight-line fit is for every choice of slope and intercept. A ball, the current model, steps downhill and leaves a trail. Each step uses a random mini-batch, a small random handful of the data points. Beside the bowl, a small chart shows the data points with the current line, and the mini-batch points are lit up. Change the learning rate and batch size to watch the path go from smooth to jittery, from slow to fast, or from zigzagging to blowing up.
original.reason: You asked to change the learning rate and batch size and see what happens. Here you can run the descent step by step and compare its path, loss and line fit as you change each setting.
interactions: Play, pause or advance one step at a time. Each step draws a new random mini-batch, lights its points on the chart and moves the ball.
Learning rate: small values give short, slow steps. Near 0.9 the ball zigzags across the bowl's steep walls. Above about 0.92 the path grows instead of settling: it diverges.
Batch size: at 1 the path is very jittery. As it grows, the jitter shrinks. At 40, every point is used, so each step is ordinary gradient descent and the path is smooth.
Readouts show the step count, the loss on all the data, the loss on the current mini-batch, and the stability limit for the learning rate (about 0.92).
A yellow arrow shows the mini-batch's downhill direction (its negative gradient); the ball moves along it. A grey arrow shows the true full-data downhill direction.
'New run, keep old path' sends the ball back to its starting point with your current settings. The previous trail stays faded so you can compare.
original.learningGoal: SGD follows a noisy estimate of the downhill direction. Bigger batches make that estimate less noisy. The learning rate trades speed against stability: too small is slow, and too large zigzags or diverges.
assumptions: Real SGD on a small made-up dataset: 40 points scattered around a line, fitted with two numbers (slope and intercept).
The loss is the mean squared error, so the bowl's shape is exact. It is longer in one direction than the other because the data's x-values all sit between 0 and 2.
Mini-batches are drawn at random without repeats inside a batch. The random sequence comes from a fixed seed, so Reset replays the same batches.
There is no momentum and no learning-rate decay: each step moves by learning rate times the mini-batch gradient.
A run stops after 300 steps, or when the loss leaves the plotted range. If it leaves the range, it is marked 'diverged' and the ball stays at the edge.
limitations: Single steps do not always lower the full-data loss. With small batches the loss often rises for a step, and it only falls on average.
With a fixed learning rate and small batches, the ball keeps jittering near the minimum instead of settling exactly on it.
Real models have millions of parameters and loss surfaces that are not bowls. This two-parameter bowl shows the mechanics, not that complexity.
The stability limit of about 0.92 belongs to this dataset. Other data gives a different limit.
